exploration.title: Pressure Tank
exploration.subject: Physics
exploration.summary: Compare water pressure and outlet speed in differently shaped tanks at the same water level.
exploration.question: Does a wider tank make water leave faster when the depth above the outlet stays the same?
exploration.explanation: In still water, pressure increases with depth below the surface. For an open tank with a small outlet, the depth above that outlet also determines the ideal initial exit speed. A wider tank can hold more water without increasing either quantity at the same depth. The pressure reading is the static gauge pressure at outlet depth, above atmospheric pressure; the emerging free jet itself is approximately at atmospheric pressure. The model shows an instant and omits flow losses, air drag and the falling water level during draining.

experiments.title: Raise the water
experiments.instruction: Choose Raise the water. If the surface rises from 1 to 2 m while the outlet stays at 0.5 m, what happens to the tank pressure at that height? Select your prediction, then Set baseline and Raise surface to 2 m. Keep the narrow tank and outlet height of 0.5 m. Compare water surfaces at 1 and 2 m. Measure the vertical depth below the surface, not the outlet’s height above the floor.
experiments.observe: Head rises from 0.5 to 1.5 m. Tank gauge pressure triples from 4.905 to 14.715 kPa; ideal jet speed rises from 3.13 to 5.42 m/s, not threefold. Why does tripling head triple the pressure but not the jet speed? Compare the head and speed readouts.

experiments.title: Change tank shape
experiments.instruction: Choose Change tank shape. Will a wider tank send the jet faster at the same water level and outlet height? Select your prediction, then Set baseline and Use the wide tank. Keep the surface at 2 m and the outlet at 0.5 m. Change only the tank from narrow to wide. This is an instantaneous comparison, not a timed draining test.
experiments.observe: Volume increases from 2,000 to 6,480 liters, but the head remains 1.5 m. Static gauge pressure stays 14.715 kPa and ideal jet speed stays 5.42 m/s. Why can the wider tank hold more water without increasing pressure at the same depth? What would differ if both tanks were allowed to drain?

exploration.misconception: More water volume does not automatically mean greater pressure at a chosen depth. Tank shape can affect how the level falls during draining, which this instantaneous comparison does not calculate.
